We heard that the Mistress <note>referring to Aunt Xue</note> has a medicine for cudgel wounds here. Could you find a pill for me, Miss?"

Baochai heard this and hurriedly ordered Ying'er to find two pills to give to Ping'er. Baochai said, "Since that is the case, you go and convey my regards on my behalf; I shall not go myself." Ping'er promised Baochai and left. That is all for now.

Now, after Xiangling had met everyone and finished her evening meal, Baochai and the others went to visit their mother, so she went to the Xiaoxiang Pavilion. By this time, Daiyu was more than half recovered. Seeing that Xiangling had also moved into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. Xiangling smiled and said, "Now that I have moved in, I will have some spare time. If you could teach me how to write poetry, it would be my great fortune!" Daiyu smiled and said, "If you want to learn to write poetry, you must take me as your teacher. Although I am not an expert, I can certainly manage to teach you." Xiangling laughed, "If that is truly the case, then I will take you as my teacher, but you must not get annoyed with me." Daiyu said, "What is so difficult about it that it is worth fretting over? It is nothing more than the <term>qi cheng zhuan he</term> <gloss>the four-part structure of a poem: introduction, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. The middle development and transition sections consist of two pairs of parallel couplets: level tones must be paired with oblique tones; abstract words with concrete ones, and vice versa. If you happen to produce a truly extraordinary line, it does not even matter if the tone patterns or the abstract and concrete are not perfectly matched."

Xiangling smiled and said, "No wonder that whenever I sneak a peek at a volume of old poetry, I find some lines that are perfectly parallel, while others are not. I also heard it said that, 'The first, third, and fifth characters do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Yet, when I look at the poems of the ancients, I see some that follow this, while in others, the second, fourth, and sixth characters are incorrect. This has puzzled me every day. Now that I hear you say this, it turns out these rules are not important at all; as long as the wording is novel and unusual, that is what matters most." Daiyu replied, "That is exactly the principle. The wording is ultimately a secondary matter; the primary importance lies in establishing the intent. If the sentiment is genuine, the words do not even need embellishment to be good. This is called 'not letting the words harm the intent.'"

Xiangling said, "I am fond of Lu Fangweng's lines: 'The heavy curtains remain unrolled, and the scent lingers long; the ancient inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It sounds so vivid and interesting!" Daiyu responded, "Because you do not know poetry, you are attracted to such shallow and accessible things. Once you get trapped in that style, you will never be able to learn the proper way. Just listen to me: if you are truly serious about learning, I have the <term>Wang Mojie Quanji</term> <gloss>Complete Collection of Wang Wei</gloss> here. You should carefully study and memorize his one hundred five-syllable regulated verses first. After that, read one hundred and twenty of Old Du's <note>referring to Du Fu</note> seven-syllable regulated verses, and next, read one or two hundred of Li Qinglian's <note>referring to Li Bai</note> seven-syllable quatrains. Once you have built a foundation with these three men, then take a look at the works of Tao Yuanming, Ying, Liu, Xie, Ruan, Yu, and Bao. Since you are such a clever and quick-witted person, you will be a poet yourself within a year!" Xiangling heard this and laughed, "If that is the case, good sister, please bring those books out for me so I can take them back; reading a few poems at night would be wonderful." Upon hearing this, Daiyu ordered Zijian to bring Wang Youcheng's <note>another name for Wang Wei</note> five-syllable regulated verses and handed them to Xiangling, saying, "Only look at the ones with red circles; those are my selections. Read them one by one. If you don't understand something, ask your sister <note>Baochai</note>, or if you happen to run into me, I will explain it to you."

Xiangling took the poems and returned to the Hengwu Courtyard. Setting aside all other matters, she sat under the lamp and began to read them one by one. Baochai urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such diligence, Baochai had no choice but to let her be.

One day, just after Daiyu had finished washing and dressing, she saw Xiangling bringing the book over, humming and wanting to exchange it for Du's regulated verses. Daiyu smiled and asked, "How many have you managed to memorize in total?" Xiangling smiled and said, "I have read all the ones with red circles." Daiyu asked, "Have you gained any understanding from them?" Xiangling smiled and said, "I have gained some understanding, but I am not sure if it is correct. Let me recite some for you to hear."

<summary>Daiyu instructs Xiangling on the study of classical poetry, emphasizing the importance of intent over rigid structural rules and recommending the works of Wang Wei, Du Fu, and Li Bai.</summary>
<keywords>Daiyu, Xiangling, Poetry, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, literary instruction</keywords>
